issues.legal_issue: An unconditional contractual obligation to perform future business work is an accrued liability when the contract is made, even if performance and payment occur later.
material_facts: The business sold plots under deeds that unconditionally bound it to complete specified development work.
The deeds allowed the work to be completed within a reasonable time, although they referred to a six-month period; the purchasers could enforce the undertaking.
The business estimated the cost of the work and recorded it as a debit under the mercantile method, although it had not yet incurred or paid the expense.
issues.conclusion: The liability accrued when the deeds were executed; it was not contingent merely because the work and related expenditure would occur later or because the precise amount had to be estimated.
issues.legal_principle: Under the mercantile method, expenditure is debited when a legal liability is incurred, before it is actually disbursed (Keshav Mills Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax). The unconditional and enforceable undertaking here was an accrued liability, unlike the future or contingent obligation in Peter Merchant Ltd. v. Stedeford. Difficulty in estimating an accrued liability does not make it contingent; the amount may be properly estimated with regard to the circumstances, as illustrated by Gold Coast Selection Trust Ltd. v. Humphrey.

predicates.income_tax_business_profit_assessment: A proceeding concerns the assessment of taxable profits from a business.
predicates.enforceable_unconditional_business_promi: A business makes an unconditional, enforceable promise to perform work in connection with its business.
predicates.performance_due_later: The promised work or the expenditure needed to perform it is to occur after the promise is made.

issues.definition: When a business-profit tax assessment involves an unconditional, enforceable business promise whose performance is due later, the obligation is accrued rather than contingent.

issues.legal_issue: An estimated expense for an accrued business liability is deductible in computing business profits under the general rule for determining profits, even if it is not covered by a specific deduction provision.
material_facts: The business used the mercantile method, and the tax authority accepted that method.
For plots sold during the accounting year, the business recorded the full sale price as income, including amounts not yet received in cash.
The deeds of sale required the business to carry out development work, and it estimated and debited the cost of that work as an accrued liability incidental to earning the sale proceeds.
The business produced evidence concerning the estimated expenditure, and its amount was not challenged; no express or implied prohibition against the deduction applied.
issues.conclusion: The estimated expenditure was deductible in computing the business’s profits under section 10(1), even if it did not fall within a specific deduction under section 10(2).
issues.legal_principle: Section 10(1) charges business profits but does not prescribe an exhaustive method of computing them. Section 10(2) does not exhaust the allowances available in determining those profits (Badridas Daga v. Commissioner of Income-tax). A deduction not specifically listed is allowable if accepted commercial practice and trading principles show that it arises from and is incidental to carrying on the business, provided the Act contains no express or implied prohibition. Profits are determined by setting receipts against the expenditure or obligations necessary to earn them (Russel v. Town and County Bank Ltd.; Gresham Life Assurance Society v. Styles; Pondicherry Railway Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax). The necessary accounting of business losses and obligations is also supported by Commissioner of Income-tax v. Chitnavis.

rule.if: income_tax_business_profit_assessment and accepted_mercantile_accounting and receipts_recorded_when_due and accrued_cost_incidental_to_business and estimate_supported_and_unchallenged and no_deduction_prohibition

predicates.income_tax_business_profit_assessment: A proceeding concerns the assessment of taxable profits from a business.
predicates.accepted_mercantile_accounting: The business uses an accounting method that records amounts when they become due, and the tax authority accepts that method.
predicates.receipts_recorded_when_due: The business records income when it becomes due, including income not yet received in cash.
predicates.accrued_cost_incidental_to_business: The business has incurred an accrued obligation for a cost necessary or incidental to earning its business receipts.
predicates.estimate_supported_and_unchallenged: The business supports its estimate of the accrued cost with evidence, and the estimate’s amount is not challenged.
predicates.no_deduction_prohibition: No express or implied legal prohibition prevents deduction of the cost.

issues.definition: In a business-profit tax assessment, an estimated accrued cost is deductible when accepted mercantile accounting records the related receipts as due, the cost is incidental to the business, the estimate is supported and unchallenged, and no prohibition applies.
